A.explanation: Gradient increases with time, which means increasing speed, not constant speed followed by deceleration.

B.explanation: Straight line of constant gradient shows constant speed, then decreasing gradient to zero shows deceleration to rest with distance still increasing.

C.explanation: Distance starts at a maximum and falls to zero, which would mean travelling back to the start, not distance travelled increasing.

D.explanation: Distance decreases with time, which cannot be distance travelled by a forward-moving lorry.

hints: Look at the axes: the vertical axis is distance travelled, so it must start at $0$ and can never decrease.
Recall that on a distance-time graph the gradient equals speed, so constant speed needs a straight section with constant gradient.
For deceleration to rest, the gradient must get smaller until the curve becomes horizontal while distance stays at its final value.
walkthrough: The lorry starts moving, so distance travelled starts at $0$ and must increase while it moves. This rules out graphs that start high and fall.
On a distance-time graph, gradient $= \frac{\Delta distance}{\Delta time} =$ speed.
At first the speed is constant, so the first section must be a straight line with constant non-zero gradient.
Then the lorry decelerates, so speed decreases and the gradient of the distance-time graph must decrease.
When it stops, speed $= 0$, so the gradient becomes zero and the graph becomes horizontal at a constant final distance.
Only the graph with a straight rising start curving over to a horizontal plateau satisfies all three stages. This is option B.
